intro.why: These patterns decide how an ML system scales, how fast it can change, and how it behaves when parts fail. RAG in particular is the dominant architecture for enterprise LLM applications.

sections.title: CQRS: origin, API and data perspectives
sections.plain: Separate operations that change state from operations that read it, down to separate stores.
sections.body:
Origin. Bertrand Meyer's command-query separation principle (introduced with the Eiffel language): "every method should either be a command that performs an action, or a query that returns data to the caller, but not both." Greg Young later popularised the architectural version, CQRS. Example (from Cloud Native Patterns): a car-trip service separates the write model (timestamp, latitude, longitude) from the read model (start time, end time, speed), letting each be modelled for its own concern.

API perspective. HTTP CRUD: GET retrieves a representation; PUT updates (or creates) a resource; POST creates; DELETE removes. Queries = read operations (typically GET); commands = state-changing operations (POST/PUT/DELETE).

Data perspective. Traditionally the same data model serves reads and writes (CRUD on locked data). Problems: data contention when operations run in parallel on the same data; complex security and permissions because every entity is both read and written; locking with shared (S) and exclusive (X) row locks. With CQRS, command handling writes to a write store, a projection updates a separate read store, and query handling reads from the read store. The two are synchronised with eventual consistency.

sections.title: CQRS in ML systems and eventual consistency
sections.plain: The command side trains and registers; the query side serves; they sync through events.
sections.body:
In CQRS-style ML systems the command side updates data, models and features; the query side serves predictions, metrics and dashboards. They are separated by event streams (Kafka, Kinesis), message brokers (RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ) or asynchronous pipelines (Airflow, Prefect).

Eventual consistency: an update made in one part of a distributed ML system may not appear everywhere immediately, but all components eventually reflect the same data after synchronisation. The command side updates models/features asynchronously; the query side gradually receives and serves the latest state.

Example. A provider releases chat model 6.0 at 12:00. The model registry updates immediately, but inference servers, edge regions, caches, APIs and user sessions worldwide receive it over the next few minutes: some users get the new model at once, others briefly keep the old one, and eventually every endpoint serves 6.0.

Reference architecture. Command side: train/deploy APIs, data-ingestion and admin APIs → workflow engines (Airflow, Kubeflow, Prefect, Step Functions) → ML pipeline (ingestion, processing, feature engineering, training, evaluation, deployment). Between them: an event stream. Query side: metrics/prediction APIs over read-optimised stores (analytics DB, search index, cache such as Redis, data warehouse) feeding dashboards, model monitoring, real-time inference and reports. Shared systems of record: model registry (e.g. MLflow on object storage), feature store (offline Parquet/data lake; online Redis/Cassandra) and a metadata store.

Code example ex1 implements a miniature event store: after a partial projection the query side still serves v5.2 (3 of 5 events applied); after full projection it serves v6.0.

sections.title: RAG architecture
sections.plain: Retrieve relevant private or fresh text, put it in the prompt, then generate.
sections.body:
Retrieval-augmented generation enhances an LLM by grounding its responses in external, proprietary or up-to-date data: fetch relevant information first and inject it into the prompt. This reduces hallucinations without expensive retraining.

Simple view: question → retriever (fetches context) → prompt (question + context) → LLM (generative part) → response.

Detailed view (a document chatbot built with LangChain): documents → extract pages → split into chunks → embeddings → store in a semantic index (Pinecone, FAISS, Chroma). At question time: embed the question → semantic search → ranked chunks → LLM → answer.

Ingestion / write pipeline
  1. Documents
  2. Extraction
  3. Chunking
  4. Embedding generation
  5. Indexing
  6. Vector store
Query / read pipeline
  1. User query
  2. Query embedding
  3. Semantic search
  4. Context retrieval
  5. LLM prompt construction
  6. Answer generation

Each pipeline is pipe-and-filter; splitting writes (ingestion) from reads (querying) is CQRS. Hence RAG = pipe-and-filter + CQRS. Code example ex2 builds both pipelines with TF-IDF vectors standing in for neural embeddings; note that for a question the documents cannot answer ("parental leave") retrieval still returns the nearest chunks, which is why the prompt must tell the model to say when the context lacks the answer.

sections.title: RAG building blocks: frameworks, embeddings, vector stores
sections.plain: LangChain glues it together; embeddings turn text into vectors; vector stores find neighbours fast.
sections.body:
LangChain: an open-source framework that streamlines building applications on LLMs (chatbots, assistants, document summarisers and other NLP applications).

Embedding typeNotes
Hosted API embeddings (e.g. OpenAI)General-purpose, for a wide range of NLP tasks
BERT embeddingsContextual: capture meaning in context
Sentence Transformers (Sentence-BERT)Optimised for sentence/document similarity
Dense Passage Retriever (DPR)Optimised for retrieval in open-domain QA
GloVePre-trained word vectors; capture word relationships but are not contextual
Vector storeNotes
PineconeManaged, scalable similarity search
FAISSOpen-source library for fast large-scale similarity search
Chroma (ChromaDB)Open-source vector database; vector indexing plus lightweight SQLite metadata storage; local-first development
Elasticsearch with k-NNVector search inside a text search engine

How ChromaDB stores data. A collection holds IDs, documents (text), metadata and embeddings. Text and metadata live in SQLite tables; embeddings are vectors linked to those records, searched with an HNSW (hierarchical navigable small world) index for fast approximate similarity search. Each chunk is one document, e.g. {id: "chunk_1", document: "Text from page 1…", embedding: [0.23, −0.11, …], metadata: {source, page, chunk}}. Similarity is usually cosine: $\cos(\mathbf q,\mathbf d)=\frac{\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf d}{\|\mathbf q\|\|\mathbf d\|}$.

sections.title: Monolithic architecture
sections.plain: Everything in one deployable unit: simple at first, rigid at scale.
sections.body:
A monolith is composed all in one piece: a typically complex application with tightly coupled functions (UI, business layer, data interface over one database). If all functionality must be deployed together, it is a monolith.

Example: a food-delivery app (FTGO, "Food to Go"). All business functions (restaurant management, order management, delivery management, payments, notifications, billing) are deployed as one unit, reached through a REST API and web UI by consumers, couriers and restaurants. External services (SMS, email, payments) are called through adapters. One MySQL database is shared by all modules. As it grows, scaling, deploying and maintaining individual functions becomes difficult.

AdvantagesLimitations
Performance: components share memory, faster than service-to-service calls
Straightforward to test end to end
Straightforward to deploy (a single WAR file)		Technology barrier: adopting new tech means rewriting
Scalability: only the whole application can be scaled
Size: complexity grows until unmanageable
Hard to understand: every newcomer must learn the whole app because of dependencies

sections.title: The monolithic ML pattern
sections.plain: UI, model loading, preprocessing and prediction in one codebase and deployment.
sections.body:
A monolithic ML architecture packages and deploys all ML system components as one application: UI/API, model loading, preprocessing and prediction logic share one codebase and deployment unit (e.g. a single Flask or FastAPI app that loads model.pkl at start-up).

AdvantagesIssues
Simple to develop and deploy
Good for prototypes and small projects
Lower operational overhead
No network calls between components (lower latency)		Performance and scalability limits
Independent scaling is hard: more prediction load means scaling the entire app
Model updates may require redeploying everything
Technology lock-in
Single point of failure

sections.title: Microservices architecture
sections.plain: A collection of small services, each owning one responsibility and its data.
sections.body:
Definition (Google Cloud): an application developed as a collection of services, with a framework to develop, deploy and maintain them independently. Guided by Robert C. Martin's single-responsibility principle: "Gather together the things that change for the same reasons. Separate those things that change for different reasons."

Why microservices. (1) Faster deployment cycles: widely cited figures (from The Phoenix Project era) put Amazon at about 23,000 deployments per day and Google at 5,500 with lead times of minutes, versus a typical enterprise deploying every 9 months with lead times of months; companies running many services report hundreds of micro-deployments per day. (2) Freedom to use diverse languages, tools and technologies per service (e.g. a photo app built with Python, Django, React Native, JavaScript, Objective-C, PostgreSQL, Nginx and Redis).

Shape: client → API gateway → services (each with its own data) + management. FTGO as microservices: an API gateway routes mobile and web requests to order, restaurant, kitchen, delivery, accounting and notification services, each with a private database and its own APIs; external providers are reached through adapter services. Real systems use REST plus gRPC and GraphQL for synchronous calls and Kafka or message queues for asynchronous communication.

sections.title: The microservices ML pattern
sections.plain: Split preprocessing, inference and logging into services that scale and deploy independently.
sections.body:
PrincipleIn ML
Single responsibilityEach service does one ML job: preprocessing, inference, logging
Loose couplingServices talk through well-defined APIs; changing one doesn't require changing others
Development velocityReported around 30% faster deployments
System reliabilityFailures are isolated; less downtime

Demo layout: an API gateway / prediction service (FastAPI, localhost:8000) handles orchestration and routing; a model service (:8001) loads the .pkl model and only does inference; a logging service (:8002) stores requests, predictions and responses in a log store for observability. Each service has a single responsibility and can scale independently.

Trade-off: network latency between services, more deployments to manage, distributed debugging and data consistency challenges. Start monolithic for prototypes; split when independent scaling, release cadence or team ownership demand it.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• "CQRS means two databases." It means separating responsibilities; separate stores are an optional, stronger form.
  • "Eventual consistency is a bug." It's a trade-off for scalability and availability; it is fine for model rollouts and dashboards, not for bank balances.
  • "RAG removes hallucinations." It reduces them; retrieval can miss or return irrelevant chunks, and the model can still ignore context. Evaluate both retrieval and generation (Session M11).
  • "Microservices are always better." They trade simplicity and latency for independent scaling and deployment; many successful systems start as monoliths.

code.title: CQRS with an event store and a projector
code.explain: Commands append immutable events to a write log; a projector builds the read model asynchronously, so the query side lags until it catches up (eventual consistency).
mistakes: Queries that also change state (breaks CQS).
Assuming read-your-own-writes on the query side.
code.notes: Production systems use Kafka or a database change stream as the event log and idempotent projectors.
code.code:
# CQRS for an ML system: commands append events to a write store; projections build read models.
# Read models lag behind (eventual consistency) until the projector catches up.
from collections import deque
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Event:
    seq: int; kind: str; data: dict

class CommandSide:
    def __init__(self): self.log, self.stream = [], deque()
    def handle(self, kind, **data):                 # commands change state, return nothing
        e = Event(len(self.log) + 1, kind, data); self.log.append(e); self.stream.append(e)

class QuerySide:
    def __init__(self): self.latest_model, self.metrics, self.applied = None, {}, 0
    def project(self, stream, max_events=None):     # asynchronous projector
        n = 0
        while stream and (max_events is None or n < max_events):
            e = stream.popleft(); n += 1; self.applied = e.seq
            if e.kind == "ModelPromoted": self.latest_model = e.data["version"]
            if e.kind == "MetricRecorded": self.metrics[e.data["name"]] = e.data["value"]
    def current_model(self): return self.latest_model    # queries return data, change nothing

cmd, read = CommandSide(), QuerySide()
cmd.handle("ModelTrained", version="v5.2", auc=0.91); cmd.handle("ModelPromoted", version="v5.2")
read.project(cmd.stream)
print("query side serves:", read.current_model())
cmd.handle("ModelTrained", version="v6.0", auc=0.93); cmd.handle("ModelPromoted", version="v6.0")
cmd.handle("MetricRecorded", name="auc", value=0.93)
read.project(cmd.stream, max_events=1)             # projector is behind
print(f"after partial sync: serves {read.current_model()} (applied {read.applied} of {len(cmd.log)} events)")
read.project(cmd.stream)                           # eventually consistent
print(f"after full sync:    serves {read.current_model()} (applied {read.applied} of {len(cmd.log)} events), metrics {read.metrics}")

code.title: A minimal RAG pipeline
code.explain: Chunks three policy documents, builds a TF-IDF index (standing in for neural embeddings and a vector store), retrieves top-k chunks for questions and assembles a grounded prompt.
mistakes: Chunks too small (facts lose context) or too large (noise, token cost).
No instruction to admit when the context lacks an answer.
code.notes: Swap TF-IDF for a sentence-embedding model and an HNSW-based vector store (e.g. Chroma) for real use.
code.code:
# A minimal RAG pipeline: ingestion (write side) and query (read side), with TF-IDF vectors as embeddings.
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer

DOCS = {
 "leave-policy": "New employees receive 18 days of annual leave per year, accrued monthly. Up to 5 unused days can be carried over into the next year; the rest lapse on 31 March. Sick leave is separate.",
 "it-policy": "Laptops are refreshed every 3 years. Employees can request an early refresh if the device fails a hardware check. Disk encryption is mandatory.",
 "travel-policy": "Travel expenses are claimed through the expense portal within 30 days of the trip. Attach receipts for items above 500 rupees.",
}
def chunk(text, size=12):                                   # ingestion filter 1: chunking
    w = text.split(); return [" ".join(w[i:i + size]) for i in range(0, len(w), size)]
chunks = [(f"{d}#{i+1}", c) for d, t in DOCS.items() for i, c in enumerate(chunk(t))]
vec = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english").fit([c for _, c in chunks])   # filter 2: "embedding model"
index = vec.transform([c for _, c in chunks])                             # filter 3: index / vector store

def retrieve(question, k=2):                                # query pipeline
    q = vec.transform([question])
    sims = (index @ q.T).toarray().ravel()
    best = np.argsort(-sims)[:k]
    return [(chunks[i][0], round(float(sims[i]), 3), chunks[i][1]) for i in best]

def build_prompt(question, ctx):
    context = "\n".join(f"[{cid}] {text}" for cid, _, text in ctx)
    return f"Answer using only the context. Cite chunk ids.\nContext:\n{context}\nQuestion: {question}"

for q in ["How many days of annual leave do new employees get?", "Can I carry unused leave into next year?", "What is the parental leave policy?"]:
    ctx = retrieve(q)
    print(f"Q: {q}")
    for cid, s, _ in ctx: print(f"   retrieved {cid} (similarity {s})")
print("\n" + build_prompt("How many days of annual leave do new employees get?", retrieve("How many days of annual leave do new employees get?")))
